cells.tense: You are setting something down at the pace it has been asking for.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: Among the things you're setting down, pick the one that still wants a hand. Offer it what today asks for, not what you'd lined up, and then stop — no follow-through, no plan for what it turns into.
cells.core:
Something around you is finishing, and your hands aren't closed around it. You can put down what's done without treating it as a loss, and the space that opens is usable space. People watch you do this and assume it costs nothing; you know when the finish has arrived, that's all. This is the shape of it when it's working — the grip opens because the thing is done, not because you forced it.

What's bending now is the small care that comes after. Whatever is left once you've set something down still wants something from you, and you've been handing it the shape you'd already decided on. Offer it what today actually asks for — not what you booked — and stop there. The next thing will want a different hand than this one.
cells.sheetLine: You set things down when they're actually finished.
cells.verb: releasing your grip on what no longer serves
cells.place: standing in a doorway where something has already ended

cells.tense: You will have walked away from it before it has finished with you.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: Before the next big idea you build about what comes after, do one small plain thing, alone, once. It may feel pointless. Keep it short and build nothing on top of it.
cells.core:
You know how to put a thing down. Lately the putting-down arrives early, though — before the finish — and it comes out looking like virtue. You give something up and call it freedom, and there's a small pride attached that wasn't there when you simply let go. The grip was opened by hand, not by the thing being done.

The correction is a quieter habit: one plain thing done alone, repeated even when it feels like it isn't working. That's what keeps a real ending from turning into a performance of one. Do the plain version first, before you set down any plan about what comes next. The plan has been standing where the finish should be. Let the finish arrive in its own time.

cells.tense: You were still holding it after it had already finished.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Take something you've been hauling and hold it the way you'd hold a heavy bag — same weight, no squeezing, no deciding anything about it. Then set it down and notice what your arms know.
cells.core:
Where endings come, nothing is leaving. You've been carrying things that are over — not from stubbornness, from a strength that hasn't learned how to set anything down. It's quiet and constant and it has become tiring, and that tiredness is roughly what you'd call your life lately. Nothing new gets in while both arms are full.

Putting things down won't come back by will. Something plainer comes first: the physical fact of holding a weight at what it actually weighs without squeezing it smaller. Take something you've been hauling and carry it the way you'd carry a heavy bag — no tightening, no deciding. Then set it down. Your arms learn first; the setting-down follows them.

cells.tense: You have already put it down, and you don't count it as yours.
cells.act: make room for it without steering it
cells.ask: Give room to something in your care that's starting to come up by itself. Steer it toward nothing — no assessing, no shaping, no deciding where it's headed. Watch what it does without you.
cells.core:
You've put things down, more than once, and by your own telling it was a decision you didn't make — the situation changed, or the time came, or someone else moved first. The release happened. Your name isn't on it. What you're holding would look to anyone else like an ending you chose, and you keep filing it under circumstance.

Begin smaller than that. There's something in your care that's starting to do what it does — a person, a practice, a thing in the ground. Give it room. Don't steer it, don't grade it, don't decide where it's going. That's the same move, at a size you can watch happen. When it does something you didn't cause, that's your room making it possible. Notice it, and let yourself know who made the room.

attempts.check: The record supports "letting go as conscious, purposeful release" but says nothing about the person's history, grief, or whether a particular letting-go was right or wrong; the reader could reasonably say "I haven't surrendered anything — I'm still holding it," which is why Too Little never says what was held or why. Too Much's claim of releasing before completion is the weakest link — it's the record's own phrasing, but a reader could say "I'm not performing anything, I'm just tired" — so its cell shows the mechanism in a moment they could recognise and lets them disagree. If the read is wrong, the asks still teach: doing one plain practice alone, carrying without tightening, tending one small thing without asking it to be more, all stand on their own. The sentence that served the writer in the first draft — a building image of a house being cleared for a new season — has been cut; it was admiring itself. Nothing in the cells names a stage, a house, a channel, a status, or any card but the drawn one.
